summary.design: Prospective cohort study of 102 children aged 0 to 18 years with suspected musculoskeletal infection, comparing transient synovitis, osteomyelitis, and septic arthritis.
summary.key_findings: CRP and ESR were significantly higher in septic arthritis and osteomyelitis than in transient synovitis (both P<0.001); WBC was weaker (P=0.041). Kocher burden did not differ between septic arthritis and osteomyelitis (P=0.874). In the hip subgroup, no septic arthritis or osteomyelitis occurred with 0 criteria.
summary.bottom_line: The Kocher criteria are only moderately useful for septic arthritis vs transient synovitis and poorly differentiate septic arthritis from osteomyelitis; they should prompt MRI rather than a definitive surgical decision.

papers.one_line: In children with suspected sepsis presenting to Australian and New Zealand EDs, corticosteroids were used in 9.6%, mostly dexamethasone, often outside refractory shock.

summary.why_it_matters: Corticosteroid use in pediatric sepsis lacks strong evidence, and this large multicenter study reveals how commonly they are given in real-world emergency settings, highlighting a gap between practice and evidence that warrants clinical trials.
summary.design: Prospective observational cohort study using data from the Sepsis Epidemiology in Australian and New Zealand Emergency Departments study, enrolling children under 18 with suspected community-acquired sepsis across 11 EDs from 2021 to 2023.
summary.key_findings: Among 5119 children (median age 1.6 years), in-hospital mortality was 1.0% (52/5119). Phoenix sepsis criteria were met by 4.9% (252/5119), with mortality 12.7% (32/252). Corticosteroids were given to 9.6% (489/5119) overall and 31.3% (79/252) of Phoenix-positive children. Dexamethasone was most common (69.5%, 340/489), then hydrocortisone (25.4%, 124/489). Use was associated with older age, multiple comorbidities, elevated lactate, large-volume fluids, and vasopressors; most use occurred outside refractory shock.
summary.bottom_line: Corticosteroids are frequently administered to children with suspected community-acquired sepsis, often without evidence of fluid- or catecholamine-refractory shock, and agent choice varies widely by site.
